guide_sections.heading: Trace the mask and the truth table
guide_sections.body:
Example 1 builds its mask from two pieces. Reading it one amount at a time shows why the missing amount ends up excluded rather than unknown.

```text
amount  !is.na(amount)  amount >= 10  keep
5       TRUE            FALSE         FALSE
12      TRUE            TRUE          TRUE
NA      FALSE           NA            FALSE
20      TRUE            TRUE          TRUE
```

The third row is the important one. The comparison is NA, but FALSE & NA is FALSE, because a false operand already settles a conjunction. The same rule explains Example 2:

```text
a      b    a & b   a | b
TRUE   NA   NA      TRUE
FALSE  NA   FALSE   NA
```

A TRUE operand settles an or, and a FALSE operand settles an and; in the other two cells the unknown still matters, so R reports NA. Vectorized & evaluates both sides for every element, so the order of the two pieces in the mask does not change keep. That is different from &&, which stops early and only accepts single values.

exercises.approach: For each expression, ask whether the known operand already decides a conjunction, then evaluate both in one vector.
exercises.why: A FALSE side makes any and FALSE whatever the unknown turns out to be, so FALSE & NA is FALSE. A TRUE side leaves the answer depending on the unknown, so TRUE & NA stays NA, which the reference asserts with is.na().
exercises.wrong: Treating NA as if it were FALSE predicts FALSE for both. The opposite shortcut, assuming any NA poisons the result, predicts NA for both. Each gets one of the two cases wrong.
exercises.verify: `print(c(TRUE & NA, FALSE & NA))` shows `[1]    NA FALSE`.

exercises.approach: Keep the missingness guard and change only the threshold: `x[!is.na(x) & x >= 15]`.
exercises.why: Among 5, 12, NA and 20, only 20 reaches fifteen. The guard drops the unknown third amount under the same policy as before, so the threshold edit cannot quietly change how missing values are handled.
exercises.wrong: Dropping the guard and writing `x[x >= 15]`. The NA comparison selects an NA element, so the result is NA and 20, a length-two vector with a phantom amount in it.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `identical(x[!is.na(x) & x >= 15], 20)`, so the result has length 1 and value 20.

exercises.approach: Combine three conditions with vectorized &: known, at least ten, and at most twenty.
exercises.why: The upper bound is inclusive, so 20 stays in, and 5 falls below the lower bound. The selection is 12 and 20, matching the starter data exactly.
exercises.wrong: Writing `x < 20` drops the boundary amount and leaves only 12. Using `&&` instead of `&` is also wrong here: it expects single values, and current R stops with an error about a length greater than one rather than building a mask.
exercises.verify: `x[mask]` returns 12 and 20, and `sum(mask)` counts 2 TRUE entries.

exercises.approach: Replace the equality test with `is.na(x)`, which answers the question asked of every element.
exercises.why: `x == NA` compares each amount with an unknown, so even the known values 5, 12 and 20 give NA. The result carries no information about which position is missing.
exercises.wrong: Using `which(x == NA)` to locate missing values. `which()` skips NA entries, so it returns `integer(0)` and claims there is nothing missing while the third amount is NA.
exercises.verify: `is.na(x)` prints FALSE FALSE TRUE FALSE, the value the reference checks, while `sum(x == NA)` returns NA.

exercises.approach: Put the length test first and join it with `&&`, so the extraction only runs when an element exists.
exercises.why: `&&` evaluates left to right and stops at the first FALSE. For `numeric(0)` the length test is FALSE, so `empty[[1]]` is never evaluated and the whole expression is FALSE.
exercises.wrong: Using single `&` evaluates both sides, and `empty[[1]]` fails with a subscript out of bounds error. Writing `empty[1] > 0` avoids the error but returns `logical(0)`, which breaks any `if` that uses it.
exercises.verify: The guarded expression returns FALSE with no error, which is exactly what the reference wraps in `stopifnot(!(...))`.

exercises.approach: Report two things: whether the claim holds for observed predicates, and how many predicates were unknown.
exercises.why: `all(c(TRUE, NA))` is NA because the unknown entry could be FALSE. With `na.rm = TRUE` the answer becomes TRUE, but only about the known entries. On the starter amounts, `all(amount >= 5)` is NA for the same reason.
exercises.wrong: Quoting the `na.rm = TRUE` result as "every amount is at least 5". The third amount was never measured, so that sentence claims more than the data shows.
exercises.verify: The reference checks `is.na(all(c(TRUE, NA)))` and `isTRUE(all(c(TRUE, NA), na.rm = TRUE))`; `sum(is.na(amount))` reports the 1 unknown to cite alongside.
